item.title: [BBC World] Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race in surprise victory for party
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Democrat Scott Colom is the first Democratic senator elected in Mississippi since 1982ByBrandon DrenonReporting from Mississippi Published11 November 2026, 23:05 GMTUpdated 6 minutes ago
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.
Only a few thousand votes separated Colom from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The margin was so close that the race could not be called until more than a week after election day, as local officials counted every single ballot that had arrived before the deadline.
Colon won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.
Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.
"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.
The result means the Democratic majority in the Senate is now 55 seats, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.
It also wipes away a Republican winning streak in Mississippi that dates back to 1982.
The Mississippi contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections as the party won control of both the House and the Senate.
It has won Senate seats in numerous Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.
Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.

item.title: [ABC News World] After 40 years, Chilean mother reunites with two children stolen during dictatorship
item.description:
After 40 years, Chilean mother reunites with two children stolen during dictatorship
Teresita de Jesús Padilla has reunited with her two sons after they were taken from her in Chile four decades agoByNAYARA BATSCHKE Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 5:37 PM
Share
SANTIAGO, Chile -- Four decades after a brutal separation, Teresita de Jesús Padilla was able to embrace two of her children again, after they were taken from her native Chile by hospital workers in one of the thousands of illegal adoptions under the late Gen. Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship.
“God gave me back my children, whom I thought I had lost forever,” Padilla said moments after meeting Tim Rolnick and Travis Murdoch, 41 and 37, respectively, during their reunion in Santiago, Chile's capital.
The brothers, along with Travis's twin, were taken from their biological mother while she was still in the hospital. Their case is part of one of Chile's darkest chapters when child-trafficking coincided with many other human rights violations during Pinochet's 17-year reign. During the dictatorship, at least 3,095 people were killed or forcibly disappeared, according to government figures, and tens of thousands more were tortured or jailed for political reasons.
Both of Padilla's children grew up in the United States. They knew they were adopted but were unaware of the shadowy history behind their origins.
“It felt almost like I've known Teresita my whole life. I just felt a connection,” Rolnick said after reuniting with his biological mother. “It’s definitely something I will remember for the rest of my life."
Rolnick discovered in 2020 that he had an entire family in Chile who never stopped thinking of him. He also learned he had two brothers living just a few hundred miles from his home in Maryland.
“It all started when I was trying to find out about my medical history” through a MyHeritage DNA test, he explained.

item.description:
Poland's president joins a nationalist march as the country reels from the Krakow shooting
Polish President Karol Nawrocki joins thousands of right-wing demonstractors at an annual march in the capital to mark Independence DayByThe Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 4:39 PM
Share
WARSAW, Poland -- Polish President Karol Nawrocki joined hundreds of thousands of right-wing demonstrators, waving red-and-white national flags and chanting slogans, at an annual march on Wednesday to mark the country's Independence Day.
The demonstration organized by nationalists came amid concerns about violent extremism after a deadly shooting in the touristic center of southwestern Krakow on Saturday, which authorities attributed to a far-right gunman.
Vociferous speeches ahead of the march cited historic and Christian themes while evoking Poland's past subjugation under Germany and the Soviet Union. One speaker denounced “toxic ideologies” circulating on the Internet. A message of patriotism resounded throughout.
As the march got under way, Nawrocki — a staunch conservative and nationalist — joined in from the back: He did not address the full crowd. Horns blared, voices shouted, and orange flares spewed smoke under cloudy skies.
The PAP news agency cited Jarosław Misztal, director of the Warsaw Security Center, as saying some 250,000 people took part, with no major incidents, while march organizers put turnout at half a million or more.
The president opted instead to deliver remarks earlier at an official commemoration at Pilsudski Square, where he laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. He addressed security concerns and called for unity, among other things.
“Poland will be a solid, stable, and predictable ally when it comes to security, and Polish political elites will build our security not with political disputes in mind, but for the safety of Polish women and men,” said Nawrocki.

Watch: Protesters and police clash in BarcelonaByNick Beake, Europe correspondent, Reporting fromMadrid, Guy Hedgecoe, Reporting fromMadrid and Alba MorgadePublished11 November 2026, 14:06 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas.
Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption.
Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields.
Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city.
Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store.
The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful". She said she was there to protest about the housing costs and that "there were a lot of children and old people there."

item.title: [Guardian China] Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship
item.description:
Nvidia has said Jensen Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded ‘without interruption’. Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPA
View image in fullscreen
Nvidia has said Jensen Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded ‘without interruption’. Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPA
Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship
Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy
Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy.
The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker’s board has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. The firm’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management.
Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”. A committee of independent board directors, assisted by Kim and Wachtell, will oversee the investigation.
The company is reeling from an espionage scandal after reports that its chief executive had been having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was also an Nvidia customer.
The US ambassador to China, David Perdue, said: “The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent.
“National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security. And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now,” he told Bloomberg Television.

item.title: [ABC News World] UN peacekeepers failed to protect civilians before South Sudan massacre, Amnesty says
item.description:
UN peacekeepers failed to protect civilians before South Sudan massacre, Amnesty says
Amnesty International says U.N. peacekeepers had weeks of warning before an attack killed more than 200 people in South Sudan but failed to do enough to protect civiliansByJOSEPH FALZETTA Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 4:01 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
NAIROBI, Kenya -- United Nations peacekeepers and South Sudanese authorities failed to take adequate action despite warnings weeks before insurgents raided a village and killed more than 200 people earlier this year, Amnesty International said in a report released Thursday.
The rights group said that the peacekeeping mission, known by the acronym UNMISS, knew that an attack on Abiemnom, a remote area near the border with Sudan, was likely but failed to reinforce the roughly three dozen peacekeepers based there until after it occurred.
Between 1,000 and 1,500 armed men from neighboring Mayom County carried out the March 1 attack, shooting residents, burning homes and looting part of the hospital, Amnesty said.
The death toll was at least 213, according to authorities, including 130 town residents, 76 security personnel and seven foreign nationals.
“Both the government and UNMISS had sufficient information and time to take more effective preventive action. Their failure to take stronger action cost lives,” said Tigere Chagutah, an Amnesty regional director.
UNMISS spokesperson Priyanka Chowdhury said in a statement that the mission did its best with limited resources to provide protection and medical care to the roughly 2,500 people who sheltered at a protected area established in anticipation of the attack.
Facing budget cuts and reduced personnel, she said that the mission "concentrated its available capacity on immediate protection of civilians seeking refuge within our base rather than dispersing limited forces across tasks they could not safely sustain simultaneously.”

Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.
"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.
The decision comes as Bessent has led a U.S. push to cripple Iran's economy, vowing an "economic onslaught" against Tehran through a web of sanctions. The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.
"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.

item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
On Thursday Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel to Moscow and Dublin to hold talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidentsByLaura GozziPublished11 November 2026, 15:05 GMTUpdated 5 hours ago
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."
"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.
After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Nissan reduces petrol car production as EV sales boom in China
Manufacturer says ‘shift to new energy vehicles is happening faster than expected’ and market is harsh
The Japanese carmaker Nissan has said it has been caught out by accelerating sales of electric and hybrid cars in China amid a brutal price war in the world’s biggest automotive market.
The manufacturer slashed its sales forecasts for China and said it would cut back on petrol car manufacturing while increasing production of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, which combine a smaller battery with a petrol engine.
Nissan said it expected to sell between 2.97m and 3m cars this year, down from a previous forecast of 3.15m, mainly because of struggles in China.
“China remains our biggest challenge,” said Ivan Espinosa, Nissan’s chief executive. “Demand is weaker, competition is intensifying, and the shift to new energy vehicles is happening faster than expected. The market is being very, very harsh.”
The company reported increased sales in its home market as well as in North America, regions in which the shift to electric cars has been much slower because of policy decisions, including Donald Trump’s tearing up of incentives for battery car makers.
That divergence between different parts of the world illustrates the challenge for global carmakers, many of whom are trying to continue selling their more profitable petrol and diesel cars for as long as possible while risking being left behind by newer Chinese rivals.
China’s government gave weighty subsidies to its electric car industry, spotting an opportunity to overtake other countries such as Germany, Japan and the US, which had dominated sales of internal combustion engine cars.

One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.
Jensen Huang admitted, external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the affair.
It said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead the company.
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.
Who is Alice Huang?

Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023.
The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia said this was investigated and debunked.

Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested himByJoe Pike, politics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemp, politics reporterPublished11 November 2026, 06:00 GMT
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boomByKali Hays, Technology reporter and Lily Jamali, North America Technology correspondentPublished10 November 2026
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe.
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.
Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.
Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.
Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.
Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

View image in fullscreen
People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.
The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.
Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.
Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.
View image in fullscreen
People search for survivors after the collision. Photograph: AP
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
